title: Ofgem on windless winter weeks: how safe is Britain's power supply?
label: 28 October 2026 · Ofgem on Dunkelflaute and storage
summary: Peers questioned Peter Bingham, the engineering director at Ofgem, about what happens when Britain goes days with little wind or sun. He said the risk is understood and planned for, but Lord Ashcombe couldn't get him to say how rare an emergency the system is built to survive. On storage that can last for days, Lord Krebs kept hearing that the answer depends on a national energy plan that isn't finished. Bingham called the undersea power cables to other countries very reliable but not infallible, and said the real hold-up is building the grid, not Ofgem's rules. He agreed to write to the committee on several points he couldn't answer on the day.

glossary.definition: German for 'dark doldrums': a spell of days or weeks with little wind and little sun, so wind farms and solar panels produce almost nothing.
The National Energy System Operator, the public body that balances Britain's electricity supply and demand minute by minute and plans for future needs.
A measure of energy. One gigawatt hour is roughly what 130,000 homes use in a day.
The Centralised Strategic Network Plan: a national plan for which high-voltage power lines need building, and where.

chapters.title: How rare a blackout are we planning for?
chapters.takeaway: Unlike gas, electricity has no 'once in so many years' standard, and Lord Ashcombe struggled to get a clear answer on how bad things are allowed to get.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you for joining us. Could you start by telling us who you are?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: I'm the engineering and technology director at Ofgem, the energy regulator. I'm an engineer, which makes me a bit unusual in the Civil Service. I lead a team of engineers. It's a very technical industry, and the regulator needs people who understand how the equipment actually works.

turns.speaker: Lord Ashcombe
turns.text: Britain is getting more and more of its power from wind and sun. How big a risk is that to keeping the lights on?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: We know it's a real issue. Wind and solar come and go, so you need other power stations you can switch on when they drop off. That takes careful planning, so that the mix we build keeps supply as secure as it's been in the past.

turns.speaker: Lord Ashcombe
turns.text: The gas network is built to cope with the kind of severe winter you'd expect once every 20 years. Is there anything like that for electricity?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: Once in 20 is a gas standard. For electricity, the government's target is that supply shouldn't fall short of demand for more than three hours a year, on average. That's been the rule for over ten years, and it's how we work out how many power stations we need for the highest demand we expect.

turns.speaker: Lord Ashcombe
turns.text: But how extreme a winter does that cover: once in ten years, or once in fifty?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: The planning assumes what's called an average cold spell. That's towards the bad end, but it isn't the absolute worst case. And no, there isn't a 'once in so many years' measure for electricity.

turns.speaker: Lord Ashcombe
turns.text: That's what worries me. On average about a tenth of our power comes through cables from Europe. If Europe needs all its own power just as we're hit by a long calm, dark spell, what odds are you planning for?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: NESO, which runs the grid, tests the system against tens of thousands of combinations of weather, power station breakdowns and conditions in Europe. The aim is to have enough supply in nearly all of them.

turns.speaker: Lord Ashcombe
turns.text: You're still not giving me the answer I'm after, and I admit I don't know it myself. What chance of the system really struggling are they prepared to accept?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: It's statistical. There's a range of how high demand might go and a range of how much power might be available, and you try to make sure the second covers the first almost completely. Beyond a certain point it's judged not worth the money to cover the last few cases. That said, as your previous witness mentioned, we've recently bought more backup capacity than the standard requires.

chapters.title: Have the grid's safety rules been loosened?
chapters.takeaway: Lord Redwood asked about recent changes to the grid's technical safety rules, and Ofgem agreed to write with details.

turns.speaker: Lord Redwood
turns.text: NESO has recently relaxed some of the technical limits it uses to run the grid safely, presumably to fit in more renewables. Has that made the system riskier?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: I'm not aware that NESO has relaxed those limits.

turns.speaker: Lord Redwood
turns.text: I've since checked NESO's website. They're changes numbered GSR035 and GSR036. It would help to have the regulator's view on them.

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: I don't know those two by number. They're probably changes to the grid's main security standard. We did recently approve one that slightly widens the range of voltage allowed on part of the high-voltage network. It gives NESO a bit more room to manoeuvre while staying within safe limits. I'm not sure about the other one.

turns.speaker: Lord Redwood
turns.text: Could you write to us about all the changes to these standards over the past year or so? They matter a great deal to this inquiry.

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: Yes, of course.

chapters.title: Storage that lasts for days
chapters.takeaway: Peers pressed Ofgem on how Britain will store enough power to get through long calm spells, and were told much depends on a national plan that's still being written.

turns.speaker: Lord Krebs
turns.text: We're interested in storage that can keep running for 100 hours or more, to get through a Dunkelflaute. Storage like that might sit idle most of the time, earning nothing. Your new scheme guarantees storage projects a minimum income in return for capping their earnings, but it seems aimed at much shorter storage. Why aren't you focusing on the longer kind?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: The first round didn't set an upper limit. It asked for at least eight hours, and some longer projects did apply. Those we've provisionally chosen go up to 30 hours. I do think there's a case for looking at much longer storage, and we've said we'll consult on whether a future round could be opened up to it.

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: The government's national energy plan, which sets out what the system needs and where, should also say how much storage we need. Then it's for us and government to decide whether this scheme is the right way to get it built, or whether we need something different.

turns.speaker: Lord Krebs
turns.text: That sounds rather like 'watch this space'.

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: This was the first round, and we'll learn a lot from it. We do plan to consult on what comes next.

turns.speaker: Lord Krebs
turns.text: On scale: as I understand it, Britain has about 24 gigawatt hours of long-duration storage today, and the country uses around 700 a day. That's tiny. How much would we need to keep everything going for, say, ten days?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: In principle, the national plan answers that. When the wind and sun drop, there are lots of ways to fill the gap: gas power stations, hydrogen, gas plants that capture their carbon, cables to other countries, paying big users to cut back for a while, and storage.

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: We'll definitely have times when we're producing more wind and solar power than we need, and it would be great to store that instead of burning gas later. The plan should set out how much storage we need. How to pay for it to be built is then for government, and perhaps Ofgem.

turns.speaker: Lord Krebs
turns.text: So we ask how these long gaps will be filled, and the answer is: there are lots of options, we're thinking about it, and we'll tell you next year.

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: The plan will set out the different technologies and how much of each we need. Turning that into actual projects is then a job for government.

turns.speaker: Earl Russell
turns.text: The longer you want to store energy for, the harder the problem gets. The technology is new and the current scheme may not suit it. Does this need some fresh thinking across government?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: Absolutely. As an engineer, I'd love to see these projects grow. But storage on that scale needs huge investment, whether it's hydrogen or pumping water uphill to release later. Batteries have great potential, but at the moment they don't last long enough for this. We need new ideas here.

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: When government ran auctions to support renewables, it kept a separate pot for very new technologies like tidal and wave power. There may well be a case for something similar here. New technologies need some early backing before they're far enough along to be included in the national plan.

turns.speaker: Baroness Whitaker
turns.text: We keep hearing that nobody has compared what different mixes of storage technologies would cost bill-payers. How will you make sure this investment is good value?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: That comes back to the national plan. NESO has been asked to set out several possible routes, each trying to balance keeping bills down, keeping supply secure and cutting carbon. As the regulator, we want the Energy Secretary to choose the one that's cheapest for consumers.

turns.speaker: Baroness Whitaker
turns.text: Almost everyone who's given us evidence says the current markets don't work for long-duration storage. Do you agree?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: Our scheme exists precisely because there are obstacles to getting that investment. It's a first attempt to get past them. We've made progress, but there's more to do, and we'll consult on how the rules should change for future rounds.

turns.speaker: Baroness Whitaker
turns.text: When will we see the results of the first round? It would really help to have them before we finish our report.

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: This year, but I won't make promises on the team's behalf. We'll write and confirm the date.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: None of the projects announced use hydrogen or heat storage, which could last 100 hours or more. Did none apply, or does the scheme just not suit them?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: About 170 projects applied. I don't think any of those were included, but I'd need to check. The first round only accepted technologies that are already well proven, so newer ones were effectively shut out.

chapters.title: Relying on cables from abroad
chapters.takeaway: Ofgem says the undersea cables to other countries are reliable and aren't fully counted on in planning, but accepts they aren't infallible.

turns.speaker: Lord Rooker
turns.text: Last year about 15% of our power came through undersea cables from other countries, and five more are being built, some of them very long. Why are we so reliant on them?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: The cables let us buy from a much bigger market, which keeps prices down, and sell our spare wind power abroad. They also spread the risk. Weather and power station breakdowns differ from country to country, so there's usually somewhere that can help.

turns.speaker: Lord Rooker
turns.text: But what if our neighbours have the same weather as us, or Norway runs short of water for its dams, and nobody can spare any power?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: But NESO doesn't count on getting their full output when it plans. And you're right to ask what happens if the whole of northern Europe runs short at once. That's why we make sure there's enough backup capacity in Britain to fill the gap.

turns.speaker: Lord Rooker
turns.text: Then there's deliberate damage. We're an island, and cables on the seabed are much harder to protect than the land links between countries on the continent. Has that been taken care of?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: Every source of power has a weak spot, whether it's breaking down or being attacked. Our job is to have enough variety that if we lose one, whether it's a cable or a big power station, there's enough to cover it. The cables have been very reliable. We've had one to France for many years. But they aren't infallible.

turns.speaker: Lord Trees
turns.text: Does anyone check that imported power comes from low-carbon sources? Some electricity bills say all their power is low-carbon.

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: I don't believe there's any requirement. Power traded on European markets doesn't come labelled with how it was made. Claims on bills will be about British generators. I should say it's not my area of expertise.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: It would be useful to have some clarity on that. Could you write to us about it?

turns.speaker: Lord Ashcombe
turns.text: If we lost the foreign cables at a time of peak demand, could we produce enough power ourselves?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: It depends on the wind and sun. With none at all and demand at its peak, yes, there's some dependence on imports, but not total dependence. You can't protect against absolutely everything without making the system enormously expensive, but we believe the mix being built is reliable.

turns.speaker: Baroness McIntosh of Pickering
turns.text: We heard earlier that London came close to losing power. New cables are coming from the Netherlands and Belgium. Could they come ashore at old industrial sites along the Thames and feed London directly, rather than relying on power sent from elsewhere in the country?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: Private developers decide where cables come ashore. It would make sense if it's technically possible, but I don't know whether it is. There's nothing in the regulations to stop it.

chapters.title: What's really holding things up
chapters.takeaway: Ofgem says the biggest obstacle isn't its own rules but how slowly the grid is being built and projects connected to it.

turns.speaker: Earl Russell
turns.text: What regulations are still getting in the way of building storage and low-carbon power stations?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: Nothing particular comes to mind. The main problem right now is the grid: building it and getting new projects connected. Building power stations is more for government than for us.

turns.speaker: Earl Russell
turns.text: So what is Ofgem doing about the grid?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: We regulate the companies that own the grid. Our job is to fund them, make sure they build quickly, and not be the thing holding them up.

turns.speaker: Earl Russell
turns.text: And what's coming next on the grid?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: Once the national energy plan is done, there'll be a follow-on plan for the high-voltage grid, the CSNP.

turns.speaker: Earl Russell
turns.text: You do have great acronyms.

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: I'm tripping over them all. Our job will be to make sure the grid companies can raise the money and build what that plan says we need, quickly, without hold-ups from us.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you very much for your time and for answering our questions.
